logline: A journey from the quiet ceiling of a rented room to Edinburgh’s great east window, then onward to London’s night skyline: looking up turns a passing visit into a way of paying attention.
theme: Looking up: attention changes the scale of a place.

acts.name: I — The room
acts.beat: A quiet room becomes a starting point; the ordinary ceiling and objects invite a change in attention.

acts.name: II — The city and the cathedral
acts.beat: The Royal Mile leads from shared street life into St Giles’, where the upward gaze reaches its emotional peak.

acts.name: III — The view stays with me
acts.beat: The London skyline echoes the cathedral’s upward pull, returning the story to its opening question.

lines.text: Edinburgh made me look up. In the flat, even the ceiling and a poster could feel like the beginning of a story. You don’t need a grand plan to start noticing; sometimes you just need to arrive, set your bag down, and let your eyes wander.

This rented flat became our base. The chair looked like a good place to land, and the quiet gave the day somewhere to settle. I liked having a room to return to after the city had filled my head, a small pause before heading back out.

The ordinary things helped make the place feel like ours, at least for a little while. I could take a breath, then step outside and see what caught my attention. On the Royal Mile, that meant stopping with my companion at Old Town Chambers, among flowers, bicycles, and the passing street.

Old Town Chambers stands at 329 High Street. The Royal Mile runs about a Scots mile between Edinburgh Castle and the Palace of Holyroodhouse. A route like that carries more than distance: doorways, voices, and stone underfoot keep drawing your gaze from street level toward the roofline.

Then St Giles’ opens around you. Founded by King David I in 1124, it is Edinburgh’s High Kirk. Its crown steeple probably dates from around 1500. Inside, the nave gives the eye room to travel: past the people, toward the blue chancel, then higher into the vault.

The east end gathers that upward pull into light and painted glass. The great east window depicts the Crucifixion and Ascension, and a historic guide credits it to Ballantine of Edinburgh. Below it, the paintings make another kind of invitation: to look closely, and to stay a little longer.

John Bellany’s harbour paintings bring boats, fishermen, and the coast into the cathedral. Bellany was born in Port Seton, where fishing life shaped those recurring subjects. The room holds both the scale of the architecture and the intimacy of a painted life; neither asks you to hurry past.

Here, looking up stops being a gesture and becomes a way to pay attention. The window is at the east end of the choir; the inscription’s dates, 1874 to 1877, identify Falshaw’s time as Lord Provost. Details like these turn a beautiful view into a place with people and history inside it.

St Giles’ was briefly a cathedral in the seventeenth century; today it is a Presbyterian High Kirk. And then there is the blue vault, holding the moment open above us. That is the peak of the day for me: not a grand revelation, just the feeling of having looked long enough to see more.

Later, by the Thames, the city offers a different ceiling. From the riverside, the Walkie-Talkie rises 155 metres above London, designed by Rafael Viñoly and completed in 2014. Its upper floors hold the public Sky Garden, but from here, the river reflections and the tower’s shape are enough to keep the eye climbing.

In Edinburgh I looked toward the vault; here I follow the skyline. The water keeps moving beneath both views. A place can reveal itself slowly, if you give it a moment. Maybe that’s what I wanted to bring home: the habit of looking up, and the patience to let the view answer.
